title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target value k, find the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to k. Solve it with the prefix-sum and hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Subarray Sum Equals K (Prefix Sum with a Hash Map)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target k, in an array that may contain negatives. It is solved in linear time with a running prefix sum and a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred: at each index, the number of subarrays ending there with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh walks through a sequence of daily net cash flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, say zero for a perfectly balanced stretch. He keeps a running total as he walks and remembers how often each running total has appeared. Whenever his current running total minus the target has been seen before, each earlier occurrence marks the start of a stretch that nets exactly the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target k, in an array that may contain negatives. It is solved in linear time with a running prefix sum and a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred: at each index, the number of subarrays ending there with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh walks through a sequence of daily net cash flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, say zero for a perfectly balanced stretch. He keeps a running total as he walks and remembers how often each running total has appeared. Whenever his current running total minus the target has been seen before, each earlier occurrence marks the start of a stretch that nets exactly the target.

**One line to remember:** Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is the prefix sum. Define the prefix sum at index i as the sum of all elements from the start up to and including i. Then the sum of any subarray from index j plus one to index i equals the prefix sum at i minus the prefix sum at j. A subarray ending at i has sum equal to k exactly when there exists an earlier prefix sum, at some j, such that the prefix at i minus the prefix at j equals k, which rearranges to the prefix at j equals the prefix at i minus k.

So as we scan left to right maintaining a running prefix sum, the number of subarrays ending at the current index with sum k is the number of times the value prefix minus k has already appeared as a prefix sum. We keep a hash map from prefix-sum value to how many times it has occurred. At each element we add the element to the running prefix, then we look up prefix minus k in the map and add its count to our answer, then we record the current prefix by incrementing its count in the map. For example `count += map.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0); map.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);`.

The single most important initialization detail is seeding the map with the prefix-sum value zero having a count of one, written `map.put(0, 1)`, before the scan begins. This represents the empty prefix before any elements and is what lets a subarray that starts at index zero and sums to k be counted, because its prefix-minus-k lookup finds that seeded zero. The senior-level nuance is that this zero seeding is the classic off-by-one trap; forgetting it undercounts every subarray that begins at the very start.

Because the array may contain negatives and zeros, the sliding-window approach does not apply here, and the prefix-sum-with-hash-map method is specifically what handles the general signed case. We look up before we insert, so that a zero-length subarray is never counted and so that we do not match an element against itself. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass with constant-time map operations, and the space complexity is O(n) for the map in the worst case. This technique is the canonical prefix-sum counting pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the reconciliation team reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows for a suspense account and must count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, often zero, because a zero-netting stretch means the account self-reconciled over that period and such stretches are counted for audit metrics. Flows can be positive or negative, so a simple window will not work. This is exactly the subarray-sum-equals-k counting problem.

Problem 2 — Counting by checking every possible stretch is quadratic and does not scale across the bank's suspense accounts and long histories. The prefix-sum-with-hash-map method counts all qualifying stretches in a single linear pass even with negative flows, which makes the nightly reconciliation-metrics job feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `ReconciliationCounter` service with a `countBalancedStretches` method implementing the prefix-sum map, and a runnable `SubarraySumEqualsKDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's daily net-flow sequences against a target, logging each match at fine level and the final count at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's flows are 1, -1, 5, -5, 3 with target 0. We seed the prefix-count map with the value 0 having count 1, start the running prefix at 0, and the answer at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 1: prefix becomes 1. We look up prefix minus target, which is 1 minus 0 equals 1; the map has no 1, so add 0. We record prefix 1 in the map, now 1 has count 1.

Step 2 at index 1, value -1: prefix becomes 0. We look up 0 minus 0 equals 0; the map has 0 with count 1, so add 1, count becomes 1. This counts the stretch from index 0 to 1, flows 1 and -1 netting 0. We record prefix 0 in the map, now 0 has count 2.

Step 3 at index 2, value 5: prefix becomes 5. We look up 5 minus 0 equals 5; not in the map, add 0. We record prefix 5, count 1.

Step 4 at index 3, value -5: prefix becomes 0. We look up 0; the map has 0 with count 2, so add 2, count becomes 3. These two counts correspond to the stretch from index 2 to 3, flows 5 and -5 netting 0, and the stretch from index 0 to 3, flows 1, -1, 5, -5 netting 0. We record prefix 0, now count 3.

Step 5 at index 4, value 3: prefix becomes 3. We look up 3; not in the map, add 0. We record prefix 3.

The count of balanced stretches for Rajesh is 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the number of contiguous subarrays that sum exactly to a target k, in an array that may contain negatives, and I solve it in linear time using a running prefix sum and a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies. The foundation is that the sum of a subarray equals the difference of two prefix sums, so a subarray ending at the current index sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals the current prefix minus k. As I scan, I maintain the running prefix and a map counting how often each prefix value has appeared, and at each index I add to my answer the number of times the value prefix minus k has already occurred, then I record the current prefix.

The initialization detail I always call out is seeding the map with the prefix value zero having count one before the scan. That represents the empty prefix before any element and is what allows a subarray starting at the very beginning to be counted, because its lookup of prefix minus k finds that seeded zero. Forgetting this seeding is the classic off-by-one bug that undercounts every subarray beginning at index zero. I also look up before inserting, so a zero-length subarray is never counted.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the reconciliation team. We reviewed daily net cash flows for a suspense account and counted how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, usually zero, because a zero-netting stretch meant the account self-reconciled over that period and we tracked those for audit metrics. Flows could be positive or negative, so a sliding window was not applicable, and the prefix-sum-with-hash-map method counted all qualifying stretches in a single linear pass, scaling across the bank's suspense accounts in the nightly job.

The senior-level point I make is that the prefix-sum-with-hash-map technique is specifically the tool for signed arrays where sliding windows break, and knowing to reach for it the moment negatives appear is the real signal of experience. I also stress the seed-with-zero initialization and the look-up-before-insert ordering as the two correctness linchpins, and I mention using a long for the prefix to avoid overflow on long monetary histories. Naming when the window fails and why the prefix-sum map is the right replacement, plus the exact seeding and ordering rules, is what tells an interviewer I have genuinely used this.
